source.title: Children, but not language models, show accelerating returns in word learning

record.tranche_reason: Tests token-scaling behavior using loss on held-out word contexts and proportional returns, rather than the original parameter-, token- and compute-scaling analyses.
record.gate_note: The study fits a loss-versus-data curve and reports proportional returns for GPT-2 models. It also reports per-word acquisition-slope analyses, but these measure individual-word trajectories rather than the aggregate held-out loss named by the claim; those findings are recorded under fits_no_version. It does not test parameter-count or compute scaling, compute-optimal allocation, architecture effects on loss, or downstream task performance. Results cited from other papers are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own loss-versus-data power law, L(D)=E+B·D^-β, for GPT-2-small models trained on child-directed CHILDES text. The data budgets are nested from 0.5M to 24M words, with 20 epochs and best-validation-epoch readout. This is a new small-data, multi-epoch setting with a direct result on token scaling of held-out surprisal. The fit is a bridge to the paper's main child-versus-LM comparison rather than its focus, so it bears weakly on V1 and V5 and on no other version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors conclude that children's word learning is accelerating accumulation (κ≈10–13), whereas LMs, even trained on child-directed speech, do not accelerate. LMs instead show constant proportional returns on data, consistent with scaling laws. They propose children's increasingly efficient use of input as a candidate explanation for the data gap.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a fixed GPT-2-small architecture and measures loss on held-out CDI-word contexts across data budgets, plus per-word surprisal trajectories. It does not reproduce the original parameter-, token- and compute-scaling recipe or estimate a compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that per-word acquisition slopes are estimated differently for children and LMs in its initial comparison, then uses a matched estimator as a robustness analysis. This sensitivity concerns the per-word acceleration analysis, not the aggregate loss fit in R1–R2.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-word sigmoid slopes (κ) of surprisal trajectories cluster around 1, both across training checkpoints and across developmental runs on 0.5M–24M-word subsets. The matched-estimator LM median κ is 1.16 [0.93, 1.46], against about 10–13 for children.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual-word learning in LMs shows no acceleration in log-data (κ≈1), unlike children; this is a word-level trajectory measure, not aggregate loss scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Coefficients of variation in κ: CHILDES LMs 8% [4-11], BabyLM LMs 23% [15-28], ClimbMix LMs 15% [11-18], versus children 37–42%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Variation in word-level acquisition slopes across LM runs depends on training corpus and is lower than between-child variation.

fits_no_version.finding: The proportional return γ_LM=β≈0.32 is constant at every budget; it is derived by construction from the fitted power law.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under a pure power law in data, the share of remaining reducible loss removed per e-fold of data is constant (a mathematical restatement, not a separate test).

record.problems: The LM evidence uses a single 124M-parameter architecture and a relatively narrow data-budget range. Aggregate loss is measured on 609 CDI words in held-out validation contexts rather than a broad held-out pretraining corpus. No parameter-count or compute sweep is reported.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible aggregate-loss or other version-matched results were omitted. The word-level slope and corpus-wise acceleration-variation findings are described under fits_no_version because they do not directly measure the aggregate held-out loss or other outcomes named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: Parameter-count and compute scaling; token scaling over several orders of magnitude (only about 48-fold here); general held-out pretraining loss rather than CDI-word surprisal.
Other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer. Varying the number of repetitions; all runs use 20 epochs with best-epoch selection.
Not tested: no extrapolation from small to much larger runs.
Not tested. Other architectures appear only via a re-analysis of Chang & Bergen's published per-word fits, not loss at fixed parameter count.
Not tested: no comparison of fitting choices or of curvature away from a power law.

missing.what: Uncertainty on the fitted B and β, the per-seed spread across the 10 seeds, and fit residuals across the 18 budgets; needed to judge how tight the power law is.
missing.locator: Supplementary Information, Proportional Return on Input; Figure 3C

record.verdict_notes: The tranche is changed from T2 to T3: the scaling fit is a new small-data, child-directed, multi-epoch setting rather than a different method aimed at the original question. R2 is unlinked because constant γ follows algebraically from the power-law fit. No limits_scope label is given for V1: the narrow range and restricted measure are untested scope, not demonstrated failures. The re-analysis of other architectures uses cited fits from Chang & Bergen (2022) and is not a study result. The scaling law is cited as Hoffmann et al., one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: Only a fixed-size GPT-2 model's loss on CDI words was evaluated across data budgets. Parameter-count and compute scaling, whether the other quantities are non-bottlenecks, and a several-orders-of-magnitude token range were not tested.
No small-run fit was used to predict the loss of much larger runs.
No compute-budget allocation between model parameters and tokens was tested.
The study does not compare loss across architectures at a fixed parameter count.

The tested setting is text training on child-directed speech. The study does not test other modalities, fine-tuning or transfer; it also does not separately fit aggregate loss power laws across repeat counts.
No downstream task performance was measured or predicted.

The study does not compare fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations across parameter-count conventions, schedules, datasets or fitting methods, nor test systematic bending of aggregate loss curves.

rows.subject: GPT-2-small models
rows.operation_detail: Fit mean surprisal on CDI words across increasing training-data budgets.

conditions.value: English CHILDES; nested budgets from 0.5M to 24M words
609 CDI words, using about 50 held-out validation contexts

rows.measure: Mean surprisal L(D) on CDI words as a function of data budget D
rows.locator: Supplementary Information, Proportional Return on Input
rows.note: This is an aggregate loss fit on held-out word contexts, not a general pretraining validation loss across all text. The tested budget range is 0.5M–24M words, about a 48-fold span.
rows.check: The 'baseline' E≈2.94 nats is a fitted parameter of the power law (the irreducible floor), not an independent baseline or control. The loss is mean surprisal on 609 CDI words in about 50 held-out contexts, not general held-out pretraining loss. The span is about 48-fold (0.5M–24M words). The model size is fixed at 124M, so data is the bottleneck. No uncertainty on B or β is reported, and the text does not say whether the fit uses all 10 seeds per budget. The V5 link rests only on the multi-epoch (20-epoch, repeated-data) regime; the study does not vary repetition.

rows.subject: GPT-2-small models
rows.operation_detail: Calculate proportional return from the fitted loss-versus-data curve.

conditions.value: English CHILDES; data-budget sweep from 0.5M to 24M words

rows.locator: Supplementary Information, Proportional Return on Input; Figure 3C
rows.note: The authors derive this result from the fitted power law; it is not a separate parameter- or compute-scaling result.
rows.check: The proportional return γ_LM=β is derived algebraically from the fitted power law in R1, so it is constant by construction. It is a restatement of R1, not independent evidence on any version. Figure 3C plots LM trajectories, but the text gives no numeric check of constancy apart from the fit.

relationships.condition: Fixed 124M GPT-2-small trained on nested CHILDES subsets of 0.5M–24M words; mean held-out surprisal on 609 CDI words
relationships.reason: A power law in data fits CDI-word surprisal closely (β≈0.32, R²=0.998) over a narrow, about 48-fold range (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Held-out CDI-word surprisal followed a data power law with β ≈ 0.32 and R² = 0.998 over an approximately 48-fold data range.

relationships.condition: Multi-epoch (20-epoch, repeated-data) training on child-directed text, best-validation-epoch readout
relationships.reason: The same E+B·D^-β form fits well (R²=0.998) in this repeated-data, small-corpus regime. Repetition count is not varied, so the support is weak (R1).
relationships.display_finding: The form E + B·D^-β fits with R² = 0.998, although repetition count is held fixed.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
